newsitem.title: UK: No let-up in Loyalist picket of Catholic church.
newsitem.headline: No let-up in Loyalist picket of Catholic church.

text.p: Stout steel shutters guarded the windows of Harryville's Catholic church on Sunday as Northern Ireland awaited the climax of a Protestant "marching season".
The church at Harryville, on the edge of Ballymena, has been the target for extremists for 40 weeks despite widespread condemnation by most of the province's Protestants and Catholics.

Harryville, where pro-British flags fly from the upstairs windows of working-class Protestant homes, is a byword for a bitter sectarianism that festers in the British province and often explodes in violence.

A small group of "Loyalists", whose behaviour has been firmly repudiated by the chief Protestant marching fraternity, the pro-British Orange Order, assemble for two hours each Saturday night opposite the church.
They are protesting about a police ban on a pro-British parade in a nearby Irish nationalist village, which they say prevented Protestants from attending a church service there.
"Sometimes they can be very quiet, other times they are singing, jeering and shouting," said a Catholic woman apprehensively on Saturday night.
Fifteen police vehicles were drawn up bumper to bumper in front of the Loyalists to ensure free passage for Catholic churchgoers. More police vehicles were in side-streets.
Many Protestants are appalled by the church picket.
Ballymena's Protestant major has joined a small clutch of non-Catholics who each week gather inside the church railings to show sympathy and defend the Catholics' right to worship.

But Harryville is just another pressure point in a volatile season. All year the province is a tinderbox because of sporadic violence by rival guerrillas split over the future of British rule. The annual "marching season" adds to the instability.
The Orangemen who march in tens of thousands across the province on July 12, their main parades day, say they do so to celebrate their religion and their British links.
But Catholic anger rises when the parades they regard as anti-Irish and provocative go through their zones.
At Drumcree near the town of Portadown, Protestants and Catholics are polarised over an annual parade due on July 6.
Last year Orangemen were banned from the Drumcree Catholic zone. After riots and road blockades by Protestants across the province, police did a U-turn after four days. Catholic gangs then rioted.
Sectarian violence raged for more than a week with police being hit by both sides. Two Catholics were killed. Politicians and church leaders said the province was brought to the brink of disaster.
But this year both sides are making rival plans that many fear could spark a re-run of last year's havoc.
The Orange Order, determined not to give in to what it sees as Irish republican agitation, aims to hold a march from Drumcree that will pass through a strongly nationalist zone.
Catholic nationalists plan to stage an open air "street festival" when the march is due. "Orangemen" say that could lead to clashes, but the Catholics deny trying to be provocative.
Observers on both sides say that despite arms-length mediation the dispute is falling into a gloomy pattern of previous years.
